pass_a_gloss: Elisha was of that sort: though not present bodily he accompanied Gehazi spiritually and asked whether his heart was with him when the two talents of silver and the garments were taken from Naaman the Syrian. So did Elisha possess this grace while Paul the apostle of Christ, who eagerly sought the greater gifts and especially prophecy, lacked such grace? I judge and boldly affirm that Paul was apostle and prophet alike. He spoke as prophet when he said people will be self-lovers, money-lovers, boasters, proud, blasphemers, and rebellious toward parents. He also said the Spirit expressly declares that in later seasons some will fall away from the faith—meaning the Spirit within him. With that gift, though absent in body, he was present in spirit wherever he willed, and not he alone but also the power of Jesus. Therefore purge the old yeast so you become a fresh batch, since you are unleavened; Christ our paschal victim was slain for us. Keep festival not in old yeast or yeast of vice and evil, but in unleavened cakes of sincerity and truth. Whoever discarded the old human being with his practices and holds none of the ancient yeast, having formed a fresh batch after Christ Jesus, has celebrated the unleavened feast; afterward the new yeast appears, and that new yeast is Jesus Christ. First eat unleavened food, refusing every vice and evil. The apostle teaches: purge the old yeast that you may be a fresh batch as you are unleavened. Among Jews, when the unleavened day dawns they clear every old yeast from the house; likewise inspect your inner store-rooms lest yeast remain, that you may be a fresh batch as you are unleavened. Because Corinth held both holy people and sinners, he says for the praiseworthy ones that you are unleavened. Christ our Passover was slaughtered. Under Moses the Passover and slain sheep come first, then unleavened eating; so he says the Passover is already sacrificed—Christ. Therefore feast not in old yeast or yeast of malice and wickedness but in unleavened sincerity and truth: sincerity for conduct, truth for knowledge; both mark the genuine unleavened bread. I wrote in the letter not to mix with fornicators—not absolutely the fornicators of this world or the greedy or robbers or idolaters, else you must exit the world. Now I write not to mix if someone named brother is a fornicator or greedy or idolater or reviler or drunkard or robber; do not even share a meal with such a one. Some inferred from the wording that another letter preceded the present one to the Corinthians and is now lost, in which he forbade mixing with fornicators. Hearing that Corinthians were upset—thinking he barred even worldly fornicators, which is impossible while living among Gentile partners and traders—he clarifies what was earlier omitted: he speaks not of this world’s fornicators but of named brothers who are not honorable. pass_b_english: Such was Elisha. Even when he was not present in the body, he went along with Gehazi in the spirit and said to him: “Was not my heart with you when he took the two talents of silver and the garments from Naaman the Syrian?” (2 Kings 5:26). Did Elisha then have this gift, while Paul, the apostle of Christ who was zealous for the greater gifts—and above all that he might prophesy—did not have such a gift? I declare, and I speak with confidence, that Paul was not only an apostle but also a prophet. He was such when he said: “People will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents” (2 Timothy 3:2); for he said these things not as an apostle but as a prophet. And he says: “The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith” (1 Timothy 4:1). Which Spirit? As if he were saying: the Spirit in me. Having this gift, then, even if he was absent in the body, wherever he wished he was present in the spirit; for he was not alone present in the spirit, but the power of Jesus was also present.

Clean out the old leaven, then, that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).

The one who has put off the old man with his deeds and has nothing of the old leaven in himself, but has made a new lump according to Christ Jesus, has kept the feast of unleavened bread. Then after the feast of unleavened bread the new leaven appears. Jesus the Christ is the new leaven. Let us therefore first eat unleavened bread, abstaining from every malice and wickedness. Teaching about these things the apostle says: “Clean out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened.” Something of this sort happens among the Jews: when the day of unleavened bread dawns, they clean out all old leaven, searching every place of the house lest leaven be found there. In the same way you also examine the storehouses within yourself lest leaven be there somewhere, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Since in Corinth some were holy and others were not such but sinners—as we said earlier in the preface of the letter—on account of the praiseworthy ones he says “as you are unleavened.” For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Seeing that according to the law of Moses the Passover comes first and the lamb is slain, and then after the lamb they eat unleavened bread, for this reason he said: Already the Passover has been sacrificed—Christ. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth—sincerity according to the way of life, truth according to knowledge; for in both the true unleavened bread is characterized.

I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with the sexually immoral—not at all meaning the immoral of this world, or the greedy and robbers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world. But now I write to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is sexually immoral or greedy or an idolater or a reviler or a drunkard or a robber—not even to eat with such a one (1 Corinthians 5:9–11).

Some have supposed from this saying that before the former letter to the Corinthians another letter had been written by the apostle which is not now preserved; and that he wrote to them not to associate with the sexually immoral, so far as the present wording goes. But having heard that the Corinthians were disturbed, thinking he meant they must not associate even with the immoral of the world—which is impossible, for one who lives in the world cannot avoid dealing with Gentile coworkers, traders, and others of that sort—he clarifies, they say, what had then been left out: I do not mean the immoral of this world, but those who are named brothers yet are not honorable.
